claims.text: At high operating temperatures, overall wear behavior and microscopic deformation in the FeNiCrCoCu coating are governed by thermally activated copper segregation at grain boundaries.
Copper segregation at grain boundaries leads to the formation of Cu-rich nanoclusters.
Cu-rich nanoclusters facilitate grain-boundary sliding under sliding contact.
Enhanced grain-boundary sliding increases localized plastic deformation and softening.
Copper segregation and the associated deformation mechanism increase wear rate relative to a homogeneous baseline state.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is homogeneously mixed, has a uniform elemental distribution, and has no significant microsegregation.
Increasing temperature during simulated indentation and sliding is the controlled intervention.
Enhanced atomic mobility at approximately 700–900 K can trigger local phase separation in the coating.
The structural mediator is thermally induced copper segregation at grain boundaries in the form of Cu-rich clusters or precipitates.
Elevated temperature increases atomic diffusion sufficiently to cause copper atoms to segregate at grain boundaries.
Cu-rich clusters lower the local yield strength.
Lower local yield strength promotes grain-boundary sliding and shear localization during sliding contact.
The high-temperature coating will exhibit more grain-boundary sliding and localized plastic deformation than the lower-temperature homogeneous baseline.
The high-temperature coating will have a higher wear rate and lower wear resistance than the lower-temperature homogeneous baseline.
Enhanced ductility may produce a slight reduction in friction coefficient at high temperature.
At lower baseline temperatures, no significant copper segregation occurs.
Copper segregation becomes operative at around 700 K and above.
Below the operative temperature regime, the coating remains largely homogeneous and undergoes minimal sliding-induced microstructural evolution.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in grain-boundary copper segregation, or failure to observe the predicted association among segregation, grain-boundary sliding, and wear, would falsify the hypothesis.
